title: Sequential Memory Access Characterization and Schedule Optimization for Deep Neural Network Inference
authors: Chen, Hanwen and Liu, Yong
abstract: Deep neural network (DNN) inference workloads often exhibit irregular memory access patterns, leading to fragmented data access, inefficient bandwidth utilization, and increased scheduling complexity in edge accelerators. Existing optimization approaches primarily focus on improving computational parallelism and data reuse, while the regularity of memory access patterns remains less explored. In this work, we propose a Continuity-Aware Schedule (CAS) that reorganizes the execution order of computations to improve sequential memory access behavior in DNN workloads. Compared with conventional schedules, the proposed CAS improves memory traversal continuity and simplifies intermediate data movement. To systematically analyze traversal continuity, we further introduce a Traversal Continuity Metric (TCM) to characterize memory access irregularity and quantify the continuity of data access patterns. The proposed method is formulated using a polyhedral representation, which provides a unified abstraction. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we implement a lightweight FPGA accelerator on the ZCU102 evaluation board, achieving a peak performance of 1825.89 GOP/s.

title: second photonic convolutional accelerator for deep learning optical neural networks
authors: Moss, David
abstract:
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), inspired by biological visual
cortex systems, are a powerful category of artificial neural networks
that can extract the hierarchical features of raw data to greatly reduce
the network parametric complexity and enhance the predicting accuracy.
They are of significant interest for machine learning tasks such as
computer vision, speech recognition, playing board games and medical
diagnosis [1-7]. Optical neural networks offer the promise of
dramatically accelerating computing speed to overcome the inherent
bandwidth bottleneck of electronics. Here, we demonstrate a universal
optical vector convolutional accelerator operating beyond 10 Tera-FLOPS
(floating point operations per second), generating convolutions of
images of 250,000 pixels with 8-bit resolution for 10 kernels
simultaneously — enough for facial image recognition. We then use the
same hardware to sequentially form a deep optical CNN with ten output
neurons, achieving successful recognition of full 10 digits with 900
pixel handwritten digit images with 88% accuracy. Our results are based
on simultaneously interleaving temporal, wavelength and spatial
dimensions enabled by an integrated microcomb source. This approach is
scalable and trainable to much more complex networks for demanding
applications such as unmanned vehicle and real-time video recognition.

title: Deep Learning Enhancement for Wind Power Prediction Using Pattern Memory Bank and Multi-scale Feature Perceptive Modulation
authors: Liang, Xiaolin and Guo, Fei and Cao, Wangbin and Lv, Xingchen
abstract: Accurate wind power prediction is essential for secure and economical grid operation. However, conventional deep learning models for wind power prediction struggle to capture long-term dependencies and adapt to the rapid shifts in feature importance caused by varying weather conditions. To addresses these limitations, this paper proposes an enhanced wind power prediction model by constructing the Pattern Memory Bank (PMB) and Multi-scale Feature Perceptive Modulation (MFPM) and integrating them into conventional deep learning models as a closed-loop architecture. The PMB consists of a context encoder, a memory matrix, a triple importance tracking system and a gated read/write mechanism. As a differentiable external memory architecture, the PMB stores and updates key climatic patterns, enabling the model to capture extended temporal dependencies. The MFPM incorporates gating mechanisms and dilated convolutions to dynamically adjust feature weights across multiple time scales, thereby enhancing the model ability to represent complex relationships. The closed-loop optimization architecture is further to facilitate bidirectional interaction between PMB and MFPM, which ensures that feature selection reinforces memory retrieval, while memory optimization guides feature enhancement, ultimately improving the prediction performance. Experiments are conducted based on real-world wind farm datasets and the results are compared with the widely used conventional deep learning models. It shows that the proposed model achieves reductions in mean squared error and mean absolute error of 51.59% and 35.90%, respectively. These results demonstrate that the proposed enhanced wind power prediction model using PMB and MFPM significantly improves the accuracy and reliability of wind power prediction.
